 TO THE HONORABLE COMMISSIONERS:

           Intervenors Solana Ranch Company, Solana Development, LP, Don Al Ringler, and

CEDON Realty, Ltd. (collectively, the “Solana Intervenors” or “Solana”) (Party No. 217) file this

Reply to the Exceptions to the Proposal for Decision (“PFD”), and in support thereof would

respectfully show the following:

I.         INTRODUCTION

           This proceeding involves the Joint Application of Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC

and LCRA Transmission Services Corporation (collectively, “Applicants”) to amend their

Certificates of Convenience and Necessity for the Bell County East Switch to Big Hill Substation

765-kV Transmission Line Project (the “Project”), a proposed high-voltage transmission line

spanning approximately 223 miles across fifteen Texas counties. Together with the Big Hill

Substation to Sand Lake Switch 765-kV Transmission Line Project (Docket No. 59182), the

Project comprises Import Path 2 of the Permian Basin Reliability Plan (“PBRP”).

           The ALJs’ Proposal for Decision (“PFD”) recommendation that the Commission deny the

Application was principally based on the issue of need for this Project: the ALJs concluded that

Applicants failed to establish that Import Path 2 is necessary for the service, accommodation,

convenience, or safety of the public under PURA § 37.056. 1 This was the correct conclusion.

           Solana’s Reply Brief set out Solana’s position that Applicants failed to establish need for

Import Path 2, that two of the three 765-kV import paths are sufficient to serve demand through

2038, and that Import Path 2 should be denied. 2 The PFD’s need findings reached the same

conclusion.

           Applicants, PUC Staff (“Staff”) and Delaware Basin Midstream LLC (“DBM”) each filed

Exceptions to the PFD’s need findings on September 2, 2026, 3 asking the Commission to reject

the ALJs’ recommendation and instead find that Import Path 2 is necessary under PURA §

37.056(a). This Reply responds to the need-related arguments raised in those Exceptions.

          The ALJs identified four independent reasons why Applicants failed to establish need for

Import Path 2: (1) Applicants did not establish the need for Import Path 2 separate and apart from

the three 765-kV import paths comprising the PBRP; (2) the PBRP’s underlying projected loads,

because of changed circumstances, do not establish need; (3) Applicants failed to prove that

sufficient power is available at Bell County East to serve Import Path 2’s stated function of

transmitting power west into the Permian Basin; and (4) intervenors submitted credible evidence

of an alternative, new, and planned gas generation in the Permian Basin that the Commission

should consider before committing to Import Path 2. 4 Anyone of the four bases, standing alone, is

sufficient to deny the Application on need grounds. 5

 II.         SOLANA INTERVENORS’ REPLY REGARDING NEED

            A. Executive Summary

            Each Import Path 2 line has a rated capacity of 7,131 MVA, or 6,917 MW applying the

0.97 power factor used in the PBRP study.8 The PBRP’s own incremental oil-and-gas-plus-non-

large-load need is only 2,193 MW in 2030 and 4,934 MW in 2038, well within the capacity of a

single 765-kV line and comfortably within the capacity of two lines applying the N-1 reliability

standard the PBRP itself uses. 9 Using 2024 total Permian Basin demand of 8,491 MW as the

starting point against the PBRP’s own 2038 oil-and-gas estimate of 14,705 MW, the incremental

difference of 6,214 MW likewise falls within the capacity of a single line. 10 The demand

projections Applicants cite may justify two Import Paths to the Permian Basin. They do not justify

three. Nothing in the Exceptions filed by Applicants, Staff, or DBM disproves this arithmetic.

            If the Commission agrees with ERCOT’s own December 12, 2024 sequencing

determination that only two of the three 765-kV import paths are needed by 2030, 11 then Import

Path 2 is the clear candidate for denial. Import Path 2 is the most constrained of the three paths,

and the path for which Applicants concede no partial-build or independent-need study was ever

performed. 12 Import Paths 1 and 3 satisfy the needs Applicants and ERCOT have actually

substantiated through the HB 5066 process.

            B. The Applicants Did Not Establish the Need for Import Path 2 as Required by
              PURA.

           Applicants attempt to wrap all three import paths together as opposed to independently

justifying each one, a framing that raises concerns warranting scrutiny. 13 The ALJs applied that

scrutiny in the PFD, and found Applicants did not meet their burden. Applicants now argue in their

Exceptions that the PBRP’s three 765-kV import paths were “designed as part of an integrated

transmission solution” and that no “partial build study” isolating Import Path 2 is required by

PURA or Commission rule. 14 Both arguments miss the point of the PFD’s holding and the

underlying concern regarding accepting Applicants’ stated justifications that need has been

satisfied for this Project.

           The PFD did not hold that PURA or Commission rule imposes a freestanding “partial build

study” requirement. It held that HB 5066 does not make a transmission project’s inclusion in a

reliability plan a finding that the project is automatically needed, and that the necessity of any

transmission project included in the PBRP “must be independently determined by the Commission

through the lens of PURA § 37.056.” 15 That determination follows directly from Section 37.056,

which requires a showing, in each CCN proceeding, that the certificated facility is “necessary for

the service, accommodation, convenience, or safety of the public.” 16 Applicants’ own witness Jared

Gurley admitted on cross-examination that Applicants had not performed a study isolating Import

Path 2’s need individually, and that the three import paths “were studied together.” 17 Whatever

            Former Commission Chairman Barry Smitherman’s unrebutted testimony confirms why

decisions on Import Path 1 do not control the need determination for Import Path 2. Chairman

Smitherman testified that “[t]he Commission’s obligation to determine if the line is needed for the

convenience and necessity of the public is different than the standard of review of need undertaken

at ERCOT,” that the Commission “should consider ERCOT’s recommendation, but it is not bound

by the results of the ERCOT process,” and that “[t]here is no harm in updating this analysis to

determine if the current projected locations for generation and load support the permanent

destruction of private property that would come with approving” Import Path 2. 22 In approving

the PBRP, the Commission expressly declined to make plan approval dispositive of need for

the individual transmission projects. Instead, the Commission required each TSP to establish

in its subsequent CCN proceeding that its proposed certificate satisfies PURA § 37.056(a)’s

statutory necessity requirement. 23

           For these reasons, the PFD correctly required Applicants to establish need for Import Path 2

on its own record, correctly found that Applicants did not perform the individualized study

necessary to do so, and correctly declined to treat the Commission’s approval of a different import

path in a different docket as substituting for that showing.

           C. The ALJs Correctly Weighed ERCOT’s PBRP Recommendation Against the Full

experience… of previously forecasted loads coming into service at lower megawatt level than

initially claimed.” 28 Applying that Commission-ordered adjustment to the PBRP’s own officer-

           D. Applicants and Staff Treat ERCOT’s Recommendations as Sacrosanct Only
              When Convenient.

           Applicants’ Exceptions rest on an inconsistent premise. Applicants argue that ERCOT’s

2024 PBRP recommendation is sacrosanct, and that the Commission’s June 2025 Good Cause

April 2026 Far West Import GTC exit strategy as independent sources of “great weight” that

reaffirm the need for Import Path 2. 44

completed 765-kV import paths as part of its “default” base case in the 2024 and 2025 Regional

Transmission Plans, but did not independently reevaluate the need for them. 45 A base assumption

is an input a planner carries forward from an earlier approval. It is not a new finding that the input

remains correct. This analytical error is compounded when assumption is stacked on assumption.
